screens.title: IP Aliasing: Multiple IPs on a Single Interface
screens.narratorSegment: IP aliasing is a powerful technique that allows a single physical network interface to host multiple distinct IP addresses. Imagine you have a web server that needs to respond to requests on both an old IP address during a migration and a new one simultaneously. Instead of adding another physical network card, you can simply alias an additional IP to your existing interface. This is incredibly useful for service migrations, hosting multiple virtual services on one machine, or managing different network segments without additional hardware. While the ip command offers a quick way to add an alias, it's important to remember that these changes are temporary and will be lost upon reboot. For persistent configurations, we'll need to leverage NetworkManager's nmcli utility, which we'll explore next. The key takeaway here is that IP aliasing provides significant flexibility and resource optimization by maximizing the utility of your existing network hardware. content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.1›IP Aliasing
Core Concept

IP Aliasing

Assigning multiple IP addresses to a single physical network interface.

  • Enables a single NIC to host multiple services.
  • Facilitates seamless service migration between IP ranges.
  • Optimizes hardware usage by avoiding extra physical interfaces.
Temporary Configuration with `ip`

The ip command provides a quick, but non-persistent, way to add an IP alias.

# Add secondary IP 192.168.1.100/24 to enp1s0
sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.100/24 dev enp1s0

# Verify the configuration
ip addr show enp1s0
Common Mistake

Forgetting that ip addr add changes are temporary and will be lost after a reboot or network service restart.

Scenario: Web Server Migration

A web server needs to respond to requests on both its old IP (192.168.1.50) and a new IP (192.168.1.100) during a transition period. IP aliasing allows this without downtime.

Key Takeaway

IP aliasing is a flexible way to manage multiple IP addresses on a single interface, but use nmcli for persistent configurations.

screens.title: Persistent IP Aliasing with `nmcli`
screens.narratorSegment: For any production environment, network configurations must be persistent across reboots. This is where NetworkManager, and specifically its command-line interface nmcli, becomes indispensable. Instead of directly manipulating interface settings, nmcli works with connection profiles. To create a persistent IP alias, you define a new connection profile that specifies the secondary IP address and associates it with the existing physical interface. This approach ensures that NetworkManager automatically brings up the alias whenever the system starts or the network service is restarted. It's a more robust and manageable way to handle complex network setups compared to temporary ip commands or manual script-based configurations. Remember, each connection profile represents a unique set of configurations, providing better organization and easier management for your network services. This method is preferred for its reliability and integration with the RHEL ecosystem. content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.1›Persistent IP Aliasing
Configuration Best Practice

Persistent IP Aliasing with `nmcli`

NetworkManager provides a robust way to manage persistent IP aliases through connection profiles.

  • Ensures configurations survive reboots.
  • Leverages NetworkManager's connection-based approach.
  • Provides better organization and manageability for complex IP setups.
`nmcli` Commands for Persistent Alias

Create a new connection profile for the alias, linking it to the physical interface.

# Add a new connection for the alias
sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name enp1s0-alias ifname enp1s0 ip4 192.168.1.100/24

# Modify the connection to use manual IP method
sudo nmcli connection modify enp1s0-alias ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.100/24

# Bring up the alias connection
sudo nmcli connection up enp1s0-alias

# Verify IP addresses
ip addr show enp1s0
Why `nmcli` is Preferred

NetworkManager handles the lifecycle of network connections, ensuring that aliases are correctly brought up and managed alongside the primary interface. This prevents conflicts and ensures consistent network behavior.

Key Takeaway

Always use nmcli for persistent network configurations in RHEL to ensure reliability and proper integration with NetworkManager.

screens.title: VLAN Tagging: Segmenting Traffic on a Single Link
screens.narratorSegment: VLAN tagging is a fundamental concept in modern networking that allows a single physical network interface to carry traffic for multiple virtual local area networks. Think of it like having several distinct logical networks running over the same physical cable. This is incredibly powerful for network segmentation, which is crucial for isolating different types of traffic, such as management, data, or storage, on the same physical infrastructure. By separating traffic into VLANs, you enhance security by preventing unauthorized access between segments and simplify network management by logically grouping devices regardless of their physical location. For example, you might have a server with a single physical NIC, but you need it to communicate with a management network on VLAN 10 and a production data network on VLAN 20. VLAN tagging makes this possible and efficient, reducing cabling complexity and improving overall network hygiene. content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.1›VLAN Tagging
Network Segmentation

VLAN Tagging

Allows a single physical interface to carry traffic for multiple Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs).

  • Enhances security by isolating traffic types.
  • Simplifies network management and logical grouping.
  • Reduces physical cabling complexity.
How VLANs Work

Each Ethernet frame is tagged with a VLAN ID (IEEE 802.1Q) to identify which virtual network it belongs to. The physical switch then directs traffic based on these tags.

VLAN ID: A numerical identifier (1-4094) for each virtual network.

Sub-interface: A logical interface created on a physical NIC for a specific VLAN.

Real-world Use Case

In data centers, VLANs are used to separate tenant networks, management networks, and storage networks, all sharing the same physical cabling infrastructure for efficiency and security.

Key Takeaway

VLAN tagging is essential for creating segmented, secure, and manageable networks over shared physical infrastructure.

screens.title: Configuring VLAN Interfaces with `nmcli`
screens.narratorSegment: To implement VLAN tagging on your Red Hat system, you'll use nmcli to create a VLAN sub-interface. This sub-interface is logically associated with a physical network interface and assigned a specific VLAN ID. NetworkManager handles the underlying complexities, ensuring that traffic sent through this sub-interface is correctly tagged with the specified VLAN ID, and conversely, that incoming tagged traffic is directed to the appropriate sub-interface. For instance, if you need to connect your server to a management VLAN with ID 10, you'd create a vlan type connection on your enp1s0 interface, assign it the ID 10, and then configure its IP address. This process is straightforward and ensures that your VLAN configurations are persistent across reboots, integrating seamlessly with NetworkManager's robust connection management. Always remember to verify the connection status after creation to ensure it's active and correctly configured. content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.1›VLAN Configuration
Configuration Steps

Configuring VLAN Interfaces with `nmcli`

Create a VLAN sub-interface using nmcli, associating it with a physical NIC and a VLAN ID.

  • Defines a logical interface for a specific VLAN.
  • Ensures traffic is correctly tagged (802.1Q).
  • Provides persistent configuration through NetworkManager.
`nmcli` Commands for VLAN Interface

Example: Create VLAN 10 on enp1s0 with IP 10.0.10.1/24.

# Add a new VLAN connection
sudo nmcli connection add type vlan con-name enp1s0.10 dev enp1s0 id 10 ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 10.0.10.1/24

# Bring up the VLAN connection
sudo nmcli connection up enp1s0.10

# Verify the new interface
ip addr show enp1s0.10
Understanding the Command

The type vlan specifies a VLAN interface. dev enp1s0 links it to the physical device. id 10 sets the VLAN tag. The con-name is a descriptive name for the connection profile.

Key Takeaway

VLAN sub-interfaces are created using nmcli connection add type vlan, providing a persistent and managed way to segment network traffic.

screens.title: Common VLAN Configuration Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: While configuring VLANs with nmcli is straightforward, several common mistakes can lead to connectivity issues. One frequent pitfall is misconfiguring the VLAN ID, either by entering the wrong number or by having a mismatch between the server's configuration and the network switch's port settings. Another common error is forgetting to enable the newly created VLAN connection profile, leaving the interface inactive. Crucially, the physical switch port connected to your server must be configured correctly. If the switch port is set for 'access mode' for a single VLAN, but your server is trying to send tagged traffic for multiple VLANs, or vice-versa, communication will fail. For multiple VLANs, the switch port needs to be in 'trunking mode'. Always coordinate closely with network administrators to ensure the switch-side configuration matches your server's VLAN settings. A mismatch here is one of the most common reasons for VLAN connectivity problems. Proactively verifying both ends of the connection will save significant troubleshooting time. content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.1›VLAN Pitfalls
Troubleshooting Tips

Common VLAN Configuration Pitfalls

Identify and avoid frequent mistakes when configuring VLAN interfaces.

  • Incorrect VLAN ID assignment.
  • Forgetting to activate the VLAN connection.
  • Mismatch between server and switch port configuration.
Key Problem Areas

VLAN ID Mismatch

Server's VLAN ID does not match the ID configured on the switch port.

Inactive Connection

The nmcli connection up command was not executed, leaving the VLAN interface down.

Switch Port Misconfiguration

Physical switch port not set to 'trunking' for multiple VLANs, or 'access' for a single VLAN, as required.

Missing Parent Interface

The physical interface (e.g., enp1s0) is not up or correctly configured before creating the VLAN sub-interface.

Pro-Tip: Verify Both Ends

Always verify the configuration on both the Linux server and the connected network switch. This collaborative approach with network administrators is critical for successful VLAN deployments.

Key Takeaway

Successful VLAN implementation hinges on correct VLAN ID assignment, active connections, and matching switch port configurations.

screens.title: Network Bonding: Redundancy and Throughput
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond single interface configurations, network bonding, also known as link aggregation or NIC teaming, is a critical technique for achieving both high availability and increased throughput. It works by combining multiple physical network interfaces, or NICs, into a single logical interface. To the operating system, this bonded interface appears as one device, simplifying management. The primary benefit is redundancy: if one physical link or NIC fails, traffic automatically switches to the other active links within the bond, ensuring continuous network connectivity. Depending on the bonding mode chosen, it can also aggregate bandwidth, effectively combining the throughput of multiple physical links into a single, faster logical connection. This is indispensable for mission-critical servers where downtime is unacceptable and high network performance is required. Red Hat Enterprise Linux supports various bonding modes, each tailored to different requirements for fault tolerance and load balancing, which we'll explore in detail. content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.1›Network Bonding
High Availability

Network Bonding

Combines multiple physical network interfaces into a single logical interface for redundancy and/or increased throughput.

  • Provides fault tolerance: automatic failover if a link fails.
  • Can aggregate bandwidth for higher throughput.
  • Presents as a single device to the operating system.
Why Use Bonding?

Fault Tolerance

Ensures continuous network connectivity even if one physical NIC or cable fails.

Increased Throughput

Aggregates the bandwidth of multiple links, providing a faster overall connection (depending on mode).

Simplified Management

The OS sees one logical interface, simplifying IP configuration and routing.

Load Balancing

Distributes network traffic across multiple links to optimize resource utilization.

Analogy: Multi-lane Highway

Think of network bonding like turning multiple single-lane roads into a multi-lane highway. If one lane closes, traffic can still flow on the others (redundancy), and more traffic can move simultaneously (increased throughput).

Key Takeaway

Network bonding is a vital strategy for building resilient and high-performance network infrastructures in RHEL.

screens.title: Mode 1: Active-Backup for Simple Redundancy
screens.narratorSegment: Among the various bonding modes, 'active-backup', or mode equals 1, is often the simplest and most common choice for basic redundancy. In this mode, only one physical network interface, or 'slave', is active at any given time, handling all network traffic. The other slave interfaces remain in a standby state, ready to take over immediately if the active slave fails. This provides excellent fault tolerance without requiring any special configuration on the network switch. When the active link goes down, the bond driver automatically switches to one of the backup slaves, ensuring uninterrupted network connectivity. While it doesn't offer bandwidth aggregation, its simplicity and robust failover mechanism make it ideal for critical services where continuous uptime is paramount, and the primary concern is protection against single points of failure in the network path. It's a straightforward way to enhance the reliability of your server's network connection. Module 11›Chapter 11.1›Active-Backup Mode
Bonding Modes

Mode 1: Active-Backup

Only one slave interface is active at a time; others are standby for fault tolerance.

  • Provides fault tolerance against single link failures.
  • No special switch configuration is required.
  • Only one NIC's bandwidth is utilized at a time.
How Active-Backup Works

Active Slave: Handles all network traffic.

Backup Slaves: Monitor the active slave and take over upon failure.

Failover: Automatic and transparent to applications, ensuring continuous connectivity.

Use Case: Management Interface

Active-backup is ideal for a server's management interface, where consistent access is more important than maximizing bandwidth. If one link fails, you still have access to manage the server.

Key Takeaway

Active-backup bonding provides robust fault tolerance with minimal configuration, making it a reliable choice for basic network redundancy.

screens.title: Mode 0 (balance-rr) & Mode 4 (802.3ad - LACP)
screens.narratorSegment: While active-backup provides simple redundancy, other bonding modes offer advanced capabilities like load balancing and dynamic link aggregation. 'Balance-rr', or mode equals 0, distributes packets in a round-robin fashion across all active slave interfaces. This provides both load balancing and fault tolerance, effectively utilizing the bandwidth of all links. However, it requires specific switch support for EtherChannel or Link Aggregation Group, often referred to as LAG. For even more sophisticated aggregation, '802.3ad', or mode equals 4, utilizes the Link Aggregation Control Protocol, or LACP. This mode dynamically creates aggregation groups, sharing the same speed and duplex settings, and balances traffic across all active slaves. LACP offers both fault tolerance and significant bandwidth aggregation, making it ideal for high-throughput applications. But remember, mode equals 4 absolutely requires a network switch that supports IEEE 802.3ad dynamic link aggregation. Without proper switch configuration, this mode will not function correctly, leading to connectivity issues. The choice between these modes depends heavily on your network infrastructure and performance requirements. Advanced Bonding Modes

Mode 0 (balance-rr) & Mode 4 (802.3ad - LACP)

These modes offer load balancing and dynamic link aggregation for higher performance and resilience.

  • balance-rr: Round-robin packet distribution for load balancing.
  • 802.3ad (LACP): Dynamic aggregation for fault tolerance and bandwidth.
Comparison of Modes

Mode 0: balance-rr

  • Sequential packet transmission.
  • Load balancing & fault tolerance.
  • Requires switch support (EtherChannel/LAG).

Mode 4: 802.3ad (LACP)

  • Dynamic aggregation group.
  • Utilizes all active slaves for traffic.
  • Requires switch support (IEEE 802.3ad).
Key Consideration: Switch Support

Both balance-rr and 802.3ad modes require specific configurations on the network switch to function correctly. Always verify switch compatibility and configuration with your network team.

Key Takeaway

For load balancing and bandwidth aggregation, balance-rr and 802.3ad are powerful options, but necessitate careful switch configuration.

screens.title: Modes 5 & 6: Transmit and Adaptive Load Balancing
screens.narratorSegment: Not all network environments can provide dedicated switch support for advanced bonding modes like LACP. For these scenarios, Red Hat Enterprise Linux offers 'balance-tlb', or mode equals 5, and 'balance-alb', or mode equals 6. 'Balance-tlb', which stands for Transmit Load Balancing, distributes outgoing traffic based on the current load of each slave interface. This means the server intelligently sends data through the least busy link. Incoming traffic, however, is received by the current active slave. This mode provides both fault tolerance and transmit load balancing without requiring any special configuration on the network switch, making it highly flexible. 'Balance-alb', or Adaptive Load Balancing, builds upon balance-tlb by adding receive load balancing for IPv4 traffic. It achieves this by using ARP negotiation to manipulate MAC addresses, effectively allowing multiple slaves to receive traffic. Both modes are excellent choices when you need load balancing and redundancy but are constrained by switch capabilities, offering a powerful solution for optimizing network performance on the server side. Load Balancing Without Switch Support

Modes 5 & 6: Transmit and Adaptive Load Balancing

These modes offer load balancing and fault tolerance without requiring special network switch configurations.

  • balance-tlb: Transmit load balancing based on slave load.
  • balance-alb: Adds receive load balancing for IPv4 traffic.
How TLB and ALB Work

Mode 5: balance-tlb

  • Outgoing traffic distributed by current load.

screens.title: Configuring a Network Bond with `nmcli`
screens.narratorSegment: Now, let's put theory into practice and configure a network bond using nmcli. The process involves two main steps: first, creating the bond interface itself, and then adding the physical network interfaces as its 'slaves'. When creating the bond interface, you'll specify its name, the desired bonding mode, and its IP configuration. For example, to create a bond named bond0 in active-backup mode, you'd use the nmcli connection add type bond command, defining the mode and IP address. Once the bond is created, you then add your physical NICs, like enp1s0 and enp2s0, as slave connections, linking them to the master bond interface. NetworkManager handles the intricate details of managing these connections, ensuring that the bond operates as a single, resilient network device. After setting up the bond and its slaves, remember to bring up the bond connection, which will also activate its slave interfaces. This systematic approach ensures a persistent and correctly configured network bond. content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.1›Bond Configuration
Practical Configuration

Configuring a Network Bond with `nmcli`

Create a bond interface and add physical NICs as slave connections for high availability.

  • Define the bond interface with its mode and IP.
  • Add physical interfaces as slaves to the bond.
  • Ensure persistent configuration via NetworkManager.
`nmcli` Commands for Active-Backup Bond

Example: Create bond0 in active-backup mode using enp1s0 and enp2s0.

# 1. Create the bond interface
sudo nmcli connection add type bond con-name bond0 ifname bond0 mode active-backup ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.200/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1

# 2. Add slave interfaces to the bond
sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name bond0-slave1 ifname enp1s0 master bond0
sudo nmcli connection add type ethernet con-name bond0-slave2 ifname enp2s0 master bond0

# 3. Bring up the bond connection (activates slaves too)
sudo nmcli connection up bond0
Understanding the Master/Slave Relationship

The bond interface acts as the 'master', and the physical NICs are its 'slaves'. This hierarchical structure allows NetworkManager to manage them as a single logical unit.

Key Takeaway

Configuring a bond with nmcli involves creating the bond master and then attaching physical interfaces as its slaves, ensuring persistent and managed redundancy.

screens.title: Verifying Bond Status and Common Issues
screens.narratorSegment: After configuring a network bond, it's absolutely crucial to verify its status to ensure it's operating as expected. The cat slash proc slash net slash bonding slash bond0 command is your go-to tool for this. This file provides detailed information about the bond's mode, the link status of each slave interface, and crucially, which slave is currently active. This output is invaluable for troubleshooting. For example, if a slave link is down, or if the active slave isn't switching as anticipated during a failover test, this file will often pinpoint the exact issue. A common mistake in bonding is misconfiguring the miimon parameter, which controls how often the bond driver checks the link status of each slave. A value that's too high can delay failover detection, while one that's too low might generate excessive network traffic on older switches. Another frequent pitfall with mode equals 4, or LACP, is a mismatch in LACP configuration between your server and the network switch. Always coordinate with network administrators and ensure you have out-of-band management access when making significant network changes to avoid locking yourself out of the system. Testing failover scenarios in a controlled environment is also a best practice before deploying to production.

content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.1›Bond Verification
Verification & Troubleshooting

Verifying Bond Status and Common Issues

Confirm bond operation and diagnose problems using system files and best practices.

  • Use /proc/net/bonding/bond0 for detailed status.
  • Understand miimon parameter implications.
  • Coordinate switch configuration for LACP modes.
Checking Bond Status

The /proc/net/bonding/bond0 file provides critical information about your bond.

# View detailed bond information
cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0

# Expected output includes:
# Bonding Mode: active-backup
# MII Status: up
# Currently Active Slave: enp1s0
# Slave Interface: enp1s0
# Link Status: up
# Slave Interface: enp2s0
# Link Status: up
Common Bonding Pitfalls

`miimon` Misconfiguration

Incorrect interval for link monitoring can delay failover or cause excessive traffic.

LACP Switch Mismatch

For mode=4, switch ports must be configured for LACP; otherwise, the bond won't form.

Key Takeaway

Regularly verify bond status and be aware of common pitfalls like miimon and LACP switch mismatches to ensure robust network operations.

IP aliasing is a powerful technique that allows a single physical network interface to host multiple distinct IP addresses. Imagine you have a web server that needs to respond to requests on both an old IP address during a migration and a new one simultaneously. Instead of adding another physical network card, you can simply alias an additional IP to your existing interface. This is incredibly useful for service migrations, hosting multiple virtual services on one machine, or managing different network segments without additional hardware. While the ip command offers a quick way to add an alias, it's important to remember that these changes are temporary and will be lost upon reboot. For persistent configurations, we'll need to leverage NetworkManager's nmcli utility, which we'll explore next. The key takeaway here is that IP aliasing provides significant flexibility and resource optimization by maximizing the utility of your existing network hardware. IP Aliasing: Multiple IPs on a Single Interface means ip aliasing enables a single nic to handle multiple ip addresses, crucial for service migration and consolidation.. In practical terms, assigning secondary ip addresses for flexible service hosting.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

For any production environment, network configurations must be persistent across reboots. This is where NetworkManager, and specifically its command-line interface nmcli, becomes indispensable. Instead of directly manipulating interface settings, nmcli works with connection profiles. To create a persistent IP alias, you define a new connection profile that specifies the secondary IP address and associates it with the existing physical interface. This approach ensures that NetworkManager automatically brings up the alias whenever the system starts or the network service is restarted. Beyond single interface configurations, network bonding, also known as link aggregation or NIC teaming, is a critical technique for achieving both high availability and increased throughput. It works by combining multiple physical network interfaces, or NICs, into a single logical interface. To the operating system, this bonded interface appears as one device, simplifying management. The primary benefit is redundancy: if one physical link or NIC fails, traffic automatically switches to the other active links within the bond, ensuring continuous network connectivity. Depending on the bonding mode chosen, it can also aggregate bandwidth, effectively combining the throughput of multiple physical links into a single, faster logical connection. This is indispensable for mission-critical servers where downtime is unacceptable and high network performance is required. Among the various bonding modes, 'active-backup', or mode equals 1, is often the simplest and most common choice for basic redundancy. In this mode, only one physical network interface, or 'slave', is active at any given time, handling all network traffic. The other slave interfaces remain in a standby state, ready to take over immediately if the active slave fails. This provides excellent fault tolerance without requiring any special configuration on the network switch. When the active link goes down, the bond driver automatically switches to one of the backup slaves, ensuring uninterrupted network connectivity. While it doesn't offer bandwidth aggregation, its simplicity and robust failover mechanism make it ideal for critical services where continuous uptime is paramount, and the primary concern is protection against single points of failure in the network path. While active-backup provides simple redundancy, other bonding modes offer advanced capabilities like load balancing and dynamic link aggregation. For even more sophisticated aggregation, '802.3ad', or mode equals 4, utilizes the Link Aggregation Control Protocol, or LACP. This mode dynamically creates aggregation groups, sharing the same speed and duplex settings, and balances traffic across all active slaves. Not all network environments can provide dedicated switch support for advanced bonding modes like LACP. For these scenarios, Red Hat Enterprise Linux offers 'balance-tlb', or mode equals 5, and 'balance-alb', or mode equals 6. 'Balance-tlb', which stands for Transmit Load Balancing, distributes outgoing traffic based on the current load of each slave interface. This means the server intelligently sends data through the least busy link. Incoming traffic, however, is received by the current active slave.
